Flat Enough? Warpage Management Gets Harder In Advanced Packaging

Shares

As packages get larger and thinner, warpage is becoming a process-control problem rather than a simple flatness spec.

July 29th, 2026 -

By: Gregory Haley

Key Takeaways:

Warpage is shifting from a global bow specification to a process-dependent surface-shape problem that affects bonding, alignment, lithography, reliability, and downstream assembly.
Panel-level packaging, glass carriers/substrates, hybrid bonding, and HBM integration are making warpage harder to control because stress accumulates across materials, thermal steps, and larger geometries.
Managing “flat enough” will require earlier shape metrology, better material data, process-aware simulation, and stack designs that balance CTE and stress before deformation becomes yield loss.

Flatness is no longer simply a matter of whether a substrate bows beyond a specified limit. Warpage now shows up as a collection of local shape signatures, potentially affecting everything from bonding and alignment to yield and reliability.
That shift is forcing manufacturers to connect material behavior, process history, surface metrology, and simulation earlier in the flow, because “flat enough” is a moving target that depends on what the next process step demands.
The first challenge is agreeing on where deviations from flatness originate. In advanced packaging, the same flatness number can hide very different failure mechanisms, depending on whether the deformation comes from substrate bow, local die tilt, redistribution layer variation, bonding, CMP, localized stress, or thermal expansion mismatch.
“The industry needs to stop treating flatness as one global mechanical number,” said Adam Cheung, vice president of business development for optics at Wooptix. “In advanced packaging, flatness is a composition of multiple different length scales that contribute from the process itself. Some of the signatures are very low-order bow or warp, but others contribute directly to local slope, die-to-die coplanarity, surface deformations caused by bonding, CMP, redistribution layers, thermal effects, or material mismatches.”
That distinction changes the question from whether a package is flat to which shape components of bonding, CMP, coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) mismatches, and thermal effects contribute most to yield, reliability, and final system performance.
Why warpage is getting worse
Several converging forces are making warpage harder to control. AI and HPC packages are growing larger, placing more silicon area on organic or glass-based structures. Chiplet integration and HBM stacking add heterogeneous materials with different CTEs. Hybrid bonding and fine-pitch interconnects narrow the tolerance window for surface deviation. And panel-level processing amplifies every thermal and mechanical effect across a geometry in which even small material-property differences produce large deformations.

Fig. 1: ASE’s automated panel-level packaging line supports a 310mm × 310mm format.
At the panel scale, the entire material stack drives warpage. That makes materials selection and process sequencing inseparable. Every polymer in the stack has its own transition temperature. Every metal layer has its own CTE, thickness, and pattern density. Every cure step can introduce residual stress before the next layer is added. The result is a structure whose mechanical state at any given moment reflects the entire thermal and chemical history that preceded it.
The transition from wafer to panel is where those interdependencies become hardest to manage. What works on a 300mm wafer does not automatically scale to larger rectangular panels. Coating uniformity and stress distribution both become more difficult to control over a larger area, and the cumulative effect of mismatched materials compounds across a geometry that offers no natural boundary to contain it. Perhaps these are some of the reasons the industry is starting small, with 310 x 310mm panels.
“Going from wafer to panel creates material stability issues from non-uniform coating and managing higher stress and warpage levels,” said Hamed Gholami Derami, business development engineer for packaging solutions at Brewer Science. “New temporary bonding materials with improved thermal and mechanical stability are needed for panel-level packaging.”
That constraint becomes especially acute for HBM applications, where DRAM dies must be thinned aggressively. The total thickness variation of the temporary bonding layer sets the floor for how uniformly that thinning can be achieved, and any non-uniformity introduced there can propagate into subsequent process steps.
Measuring shape, not just bow
Traditional warpage metrology can detect warping in a package. But advanced packaging increasingly needs “shape metrology,” the dense surface data that can connect deformation signatures to process fingerprints and yield outcomes. Getting more data points across the surface — and early enough to take action — matters more than sharpening any single measurement. A high-resolution tool that samples sparsely can miss the shape signatures that determine whether a package will bond, align, or yield correctly.
“Older flatness metrics are not enough,” said Cheung. “That’s why we develop a high-density data map for the wafer itself, and in the future, the panel. It is designed to fully describe whether these vertically integrated systems can ultimately perform in a bondable way, in an alignable way, and in a reliable way, and then have high yield.”
The value is not simply seeing that a package has warped. It is in collecting enough surface data to translate raw measurements into process intelligence and identifying which signatures are process-induced, where in the flow they originate, and what corrective action is needed.
The catch is that shape metrology becomes useful only when it is correlated with device characterization and converted into a controllable action plan. Most metrology today is target-based. It checks a specific feature against a reference at a specific moment. What advanced packaging needs is repeated, high-density surface-shape measurement at key process handoffs, so that deformation introduced in one step can be accounted for before the next step begins. As packages grow larger and tolerances tighten, the cost of carrying a poor assumption forward compounds with every subsequent operation.
Glass improves, but doesn’t eliminate the problem
Glass carriers and substrates are attractive for advanced packaging because of their stiffness, surface smoothness, optical transparency for laser-based debonding, and their tunable CTE across a broad range. That last property is particularly significant. Unlike organic build-up substrates, which offer limited CTE flexibility, glass can be formulated to match a wide range of integration requirements.
“Glass has a tunable CTE, ranging from 3.4 to 10.6 ppm per degree,” said Wiwy Wudjud, program manager at ASE. “That’s very flexible, depending on what kind of materials or process requirements you have.”
That tunability, combined with glass’s smoothness and optical transparency for UV and laser debonding, is why glass carriers are becoming increasingly important in advanced packaging flows that require stable support, fine alignment, and clean debonding. But even at the 300mm wafer scale, the processing challenges for glass are significant. At the panel scale, those challenges multiply.
Glass also does not resolve the underlying CTE imbalance challenge in heterogeneous stacks. The more silicon area a package carries (e.g., chiplets, HBM cubes, bridge die, etc.), the more lopsided the thermal expansion equation becomes, regardless of what the substrate is made of. The answer is not forcing a warped structure flat, but designing the stack so that the competing CTEs are better distributed from the start.
“If you just pile all your low CTEs in one place and all your high CTEs in another, you’re just asking for problems,” said Mike Kelly, vice president of chiplets and FCBGA integration at Amkor. “Physics isn’t going to change. So we’re going to be seeing new concepts that balance the CTEs across the cross-section of the package.”
Glass’s tunability helps, and CTE-matched glass substrates are coming. But glass only addresses part of the problem. Unless the whole stack architecture is designed with CTE balance in mind, warpage, die shift, cracking, and stress concentration can reappear elsewhere in the flow. A glass substrate with a well-matched CTE sitting under a multi-chiplet module with eight HBM cubes still has to cope with significant asymmetry, and managing that through mechanical constraint alone using stiffener rings or retainer structures just adds stress elsewhere. It doesn’t remove stress from the overall system.
Hybrid bonding makes surface control less forgiving
Hybrid bonding raises the stakes for surface control because the tolerance window is much narrower than in solder-based interconnects. There are no organics at the interface to provide compliance. Particles, surface topology, and CMP process variation can all become yield limiters in ways that they are not in conventional front-end processes.
The surface also has to be engineered for the anneal step that follows bonding. Copper and oxide behave differently under heat, and the CMP process has to account for both.
“You have to manage that surface topology,” said Amkor’s Kelly. “Oxides want to be bone flat because the chemical mechanism that pulls the oxides together is really what bonds. It’s not the copper. The copper is just along for the ride. It’s getting pressed together in the anneal step.”
The copper starts slightly recessed relative to the oxide. As the temperature rises during annealing, copper expands due to its high CTE relative to silicon. Applying too much compressive force during that step plastically deforms the copper. The result is that “flat enough” is process-specific. A surface that passes inspection at one step may not satisfy the requirements of the oxide bonding chemistry or the copper anneal that follows. Warpage and surface topology here are not just mechanical measurements, they are direct determinants of whether the bond forms correctly.
Modeling must follow the process
Process simulation for warpage is only useful if it tracks stress accumulation through each step of the build rather than just predicting the final package state. Every thermal excursion, whether in processing, test, or field operation, loads the same CTE mismatch that drove warpage during assembly. Glass, copper, and silicon respond to that loading very differently.
“When the temperature goes up and down, either in testing, manufacturing, or deployment, we know the effect of CTE,” said Lang Lin, principal product manager at Synopsys. “We are talking about glass, copper, and silicon, which have very different CTEs. Those are totally different materials, and thermal cycling can create major cracking and reliability concerns, especially around how much stress the glass can tolerate during those thermal cycle events.”
That is where process simulation becomes more difficult. The model has to take material properties as inputs and track how stress accumulates across each step of the build. But there is a persistent gap between what the simulation needs and what manufacturers are willing to provide. A substrate supplier’s process recipe and exact material formulation are competitive assets, and sharing them with a third-party simulation tool is not straightforward.
“Our simulation tool needs the substrate manufacturers’ material properties information,” said Lin. “These may include the measurement-calibrated material properties for building encrypted technology files.”
Without that correlation, most models rely on generic material libraries that are still useful for understanding relative stress behaviors and testing design directions, but which are less precise for predicting actual process outcomes. The practical advice is to run the simulation with the best available material data before committing to a physical experiment.
Correction strategies: Flatten, compensate, or redesign
Once warpage is measured and understood, manufacturers face a choice — try to eliminate it, work around it, or design the process so it arrives at the right shape at the right moment. Each approach has a different cost and a different set of tradeoffs, and most production flows use some combination of all three.
The most direct mechanical approach is physical constraint, such as vacuum chucks that pull a warped substrate flat during lithography or bonding, or stiffener rings and retainer structures that resist deformation during thermal excursions. These are widely used and often effective, but they have limits. A vacuum chuck cannot hold a substrate that has warped beyond a certain threshold without creating contact problems that affect the process, and stiffeners that constrain a package from deforming do not eliminate the stress. They redistribute it, often concentrating it at solder joints or other reliability-critical interfaces.
A second approach is compensation — measuring the surface shape and adjusting subsequent process steps accordingly. Lithography tools can apply corrections to the exposure field based on measured bow. Die placement equipment can offset pick-and-place coordinates based on a surface map. The assumption is not that the package will be flat, but that its shape is known well enough to make corrections in the next step. This is where high-density surface metrology becomes directly actionable. It’s no longer just a quality check. It’s an input to the process control loop.
The third approach, and the one the industry is increasingly moving toward, is redesigning the stack and the thermal process so that warpage is minimized structurally rather than corrected after the fact.
Thinning the silicon is one example. A thinner die is mechanically weaker as a low-CTE stiffener, meaning the rest of the material stack has greater influence on the final shape and can be engineered to produce a flatter result. The tradeoff is thermal. Thinner silicon manages lateral heat spreading less effectively, which is a real constraint for high-power data center devices.
“You make the impact of the low-CTE silicon less if there’s thinner silicon to permit some warpage,” said Kelly. “In the extreme, you can make it super thin, but then it’s just going to follow the shape of whatever it’s attached to.”
The most sophisticated approach is engineering the thermal profile of the fabrication process itself to minimize stress at operating temperature rather than at room temperature. Most packages are assembled and measured at room temperature, but they run at 90 to 100 degrees Celsius, or higher. During fabrication, every cure step, lamination, and thermal cycle leaves residual stress in the stack. If the fabrication process is designed deliberately, the thermal expansion at operating temperature could counteract those residual stresses rather than add to them, leaving the package in a more balanced mechanical state when it is actually operating in the field.
The catch is that a package optimized this way could measure worse at room temperature than one built to conventional thermal profiles. It may fall outside standard bow or flatness specifications on the inspection bench even though it performs correctly in the field. That is a direct challenge to how acceptance criteria are written today, which were developed around room-temperature measurement and the assumption that a flatter package at assembly is always better.
As operating temperatures rise with AI workloads, the industry may need to reconsider whether room-temperature flatness is the right metric. The goal is not a package that is flat on the assembly line. It is a package that is flat, or at least within tolerance, where it matters, at the temperature and load conditions of field operation.
“You’re going to see more people working on stress/strain profiles that are optimized for operating temperature rather than room temperature,” said Kelly. “A package might have more initial stress than you want when it comes off the line, but by the time it ramps up to 90 or 100 degrees in operation, it’s actually in a lower stress state. That’s the goal — managing the thermal history during fabrication so the package arrives at its best mechanical condition when it’s actually running. Of course, this presumes that you can pass JEDEC package-level reliability testing, which also covers the temperature extremes.”
These correction strategies depend on earlier measurements with more information. A simple bow number at the end of the line tells you whether you passed or failed. A dense surface map taken at each process handoff tells you which step created the problem, how it evolved, and what the next step needs to account for.
“It’s not just flatness that helps customers solve their manufacturability issues,” said Wooptix’ Cheung. “Certain shape methodologies can help them debug process issues. Manufacturers are suffering from these exotic structures and have to deal with them through metrology, and shape would be the most direct way of addressing such a challenge.”
What “flat enough” actually means
The answer to the question of what “flat enough” looks like is not a universal number. It depends on the next step in the process flow. A package that meets a simple bow specification may still cause problems in hybrid bonding, where local oxide surface conditions, copper recess, particles, and nanoscale topography all affect whether the bond forms correctly. A panel that appears acceptable after RDL deposition may have accumulated sufficient residual stress to cause die shift during the next thermal excursion. A substrate that is flat at room temperature may be anything but flat at operating temperature, which is what really matters.
The more useful framing, as the industry is learning, is whether the current shape of a package is compatible with everything that has to happen next, and whether that shape can be measured early enough, with enough spatial density and process context, to allow corrections before the next step locks in the deformation permanently. That is the shift the industry is navigating, from flatness as a pass/fail inspection checkpoint to shape as a continuous variable in a manufacturing control system.
As packages get larger, thinner, and more heterogeneous, the cost of getting that question wrong rises sharply. A panel loaded with chiplets and HBM, costing tens of thousands of dollars per unit, leaves little margin for a warpage-driven yield problem discovered late in the process. The pressure to understand and manage shape earlier, through the integration of materials, process design, metrology, and simulation, is only going to increase.
